Manoah
mă-nō'ăh
n. (a Danite of Zorah, father of Samson — the man who asked to be taught how to raise the child before the child was born)
From Hebrew Manoach, “rest” or “resting place”, from nuach, to rest — the same root as Noah. It is an unexpected name for the father of the least restful man in the Old Testament.

Biblical Definition

Manoah is introduced in the plainest terms: “there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not” (Jdg 13:2). The angel of the LORD appeared to the wife, not to him, and told her she would conceive a Nazarite from the womb. Manoah's response is the finest thing recorded of him and one of the best prayers a father ever prayed: “Then Manoah intreated the LORD, and said, O my Lord, let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born” (Jdg 13:8). He did not ask for a sign, a fortune, or a guarantee; he asked for instruction in how to bring the boy up. God granted it, and the angel came again, and repeated what He had already said — the mother's diet, the child's vow — adding nothing, because the instruction had already been complete. When Manoah pressed for a name he was told it was secret, and when the flame went up from the altar and the angel went up in it, he fell on his face and said, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God” (Jdg 13:22). His wife reasoned him out of it. At the end of Samson's life his brethren carried him home and buried him “in the buryingplace of Manoah his father” (Jdg 16:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Manoah; in sacred history he is a man of Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, the father of Samson.

expand to see more

MANOAH, n. A Danite of Zorah, the father of Samson; the name signifies rest.

His wife being barren, the angel of the Lord appeared to her and promised a son.

Manoah entreated that the man of God might come again and teach them how to order the child.

He offered a kid with a meat offering upon a rock unto the Lord, and the angel ascended in the flame.

Samson was buried in the buryingplace of Manoah his father, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Key Scripture

Jdg 13:2 — "And there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not."

Jdg 13:8 — "Then Manoah intreated the LORD, and said, O my Lord, let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born."

Jdg 13:22 — "And Manoah said unto his wife, We shall surely die, because we have seen God."

Jdg 16:31 — "Then his brethren and all the house of his father came down, and took him, and brought him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the buryingplace of Manoah his father. And he judged Israel twenty years."

Modern Corruption

Parenting is treated as a matter of technique to be researched; Manoah asked God for the ordering of a child and received a repetition of what had already been revealed, because the instruction was already given.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the shape of God's answer to Jdg 13:8. Manoah wanted to be taught how to order the child, and God sent the messenger back, and the messenger said what he had said before and no more: let her beware of wine and unclean things and observe all that was commanded. There was no additional revelation because none was needed. The pattern holds for Christian parents, who are drowning in method and short on the one thing given: “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and the daily catechising of Deu 6:7 — talking of the words of God sitting in the house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. The prayer was right and the answer was the word already spoken.

The second thing is the marriage, and it is quietly instructive. The angel came to the wife twice; Manoah had to ask to be included. She is the one who reasons clearly when he panics about dying — if the LORD were pleased to kill us, He would not have received an offering at our hands nor told us all this. She is the theologian in the house at that moment, and Scripture records it without embarrassment and without unsettling anything about the order of the home. Headship is not the claim that a husband is always the clearest thinker in the room. Manoah led his house to the altar; his wife steadied him when he was afraid; and the Holy Ghost wrote both down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Manoach (H4495), rest, from nuach (H5117), to rest; nazir (H5139), a Nazarite; mishpat (H4941), the manner or ordering.

expand to see more

Hebrew Manoach (H4495) — Manoah, “rest”; from the same root as the name Noah.

Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to rest, settle down; the word of the ark resting on Ararat.

Hebrew nazir (H5139) — a Nazarite, one separated by vow; Samson was one from the womb.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, manner, ordering; “how shall we order the child?” (Jdg 13:12).

Hebrew pil'i (H6383) — wonderful, secret; the angel's answer about his name (Jdg 13:18), and a title of Christ in Isa 9:6.

Usage

"“His wife was barren, and bare not” — how a deliverer's story begins."

"“Teach us what we shall do unto the child” — the prayer of a father before a birth."

"“We shall surely die, because we have seen God” — fear answered by a wife's plain reasoning."
